framework.name: Next Generation Science Standards (Illinois Learning Standards for Science)
framework.note: Codes are NGSS performance expectations (grade or band, discipline, number) as adopted in the Illinois Learning Standards for Science; alignment is the course author's judgment, not a certification.

standards.text: Investigate how different strengths and directions of pushes and pulls change an object's motion.
Analyze data to judge whether a design using a push or pull changes an object's speed or direction as intended.
Describe and classify materials by observable properties such as color, texture and hardness.
Test materials to decide which properties suit them for a given purpose.
Use evidence to show an object built from small pieces can be taken apart and rebuilt into something new.
Argue from evidence that some heating and cooling changes reverse and some do not.
Investigate to show that vibrating materials make sound and sound can make materials vibrate.
Use observations to explain that objects are seen only when lit.
Test how light passes through, partly through, or is blocked by different materials.
Design and build a device that uses light or sound to send a message over a distance.
Use observations to describe what plants and animals need to survive.
Argue that plants and animals can change their environment to meet their needs.
Find patterns in how parents' behaviors, and their young's responses, help offspring survive.
Use evidence to show young plants and animals resemble but are not identical to their parents.
Observe plants and animals to compare the diversity of life in different habitats.
Build a model of how animals help disperse seeds or pollinate plants.
Use and share observations of local weather to describe patterns over time.
Observe the warming effect of sunlight on Earth's surface.
Observe and predict patterns in the sun, moon and stars.
Use evidence that Earth events can happen quickly or slowly.
Compare several solutions designed to slow or stop wind or water from changing the shape of the land.
Obtain information to identify where water is found on Earth and that it can be solid or liquid.
Investigate the effects of balanced and unbalanced forces on an object's motion.
Observe patterns in motion that can predict future motion.
Ask questions about cause and effect in electric or magnetic interactions between objects.
Explain, with evidence, the relationship between an object's speed and its energy.
Show that energy moves from place to place by sound, light, heat and electric currents.
Design, test and refine a device that converts energy from one form to another.
Develop a model showing matter is made of particles too small to see.
Measure and graph to show total weight is conserved through heating, cooling or mixing.
Investigate whether mixing two substances produces a new substance.
Model waves in terms of amplitude and wavelength and how they move objects.
Model how light reflecting from objects into the eye allows objects to be seen.
Design and compare solutions that use patterns to transfer information.
Model life cycles of organisms with their shared stages of birth, growth, reproduction and death.
Analyze data showing traits are inherited from parents and that these traits vary within a group of similar organisms.
Use evidence that the environment can influence an organism's traits.
Explain how variations in traits can give individuals advantages in survival and reproduction.
Argue that plants and animals have internal and external structures that support survival and reproduction.
Model how animals receive sensory information, process it in the brain and respond.
Model how energy in animals' food originally came from the sun.
Argue from evidence that plants get growth materials chiefly from air and water.
Model the movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers and the environment.
Argue for a solution to a problem caused when environmental change affects the organisms living there.
Obtain and combine information about climates in different regions of the world.
Use evidence from rock layers and fossils to explain changes in a landscape over time.
Investigate the effects of weathering and rate of erosion by water, ice, wind or plants.
Represent data to reveal patterns of daily and seasonal changes caused by Earth's motion.
Model how the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere interact.
Gather information about how communities use science to protect Earth's resources and environments.
Develop models of the atomic composition of simple molecules and extended structures.
Analyze property data before and after substances interact to detect a chemical reaction.
Model how particle motion and state change when thermal energy is added or removed.
Model how atoms rearrange in a reaction while total mass is conserved.
Design and test a device that releases or absorbs thermal energy by chemical processes.
Apply Newton's third law to design a solution to a collision problem.
Investigate how the sum of forces and the object's mass determine its change in motion.
Argue from evidence that gravitational interactions are attractive and depend on the masses of the interacting objects.
Interpret graphical data relating kinetic energy to mass and speed.
Design, build and test a device that minimizes or maximizes thermal energy transfer.
Argue from evidence that when kinetic energy changes, energy is transferred to or from the object.
Use models to describe how a wave's amplitude relates to its energy.
Model how waves are reflected, absorbed or transmitted by various materials.
Evaluate evidence that digital signals are more reliable than analog for transmitting information.
Investigate to show that living things are made of cells, either one or many.
Model a cell and explain how its parts contribute to its function.
Argue from evidence that a body is a system of interacting subsystems of cells, tissues and organs.
Argue how animal behaviors and plant structures increase reproductive success.
Explain with evidence how photosynthesis cycles matter and moves energy into organisms.
Gather information on how sensory receptors send messages to the brain for memory or response.
Analyze data on how resource availability affects organisms and populations in an ecosystem.
Evaluate competing design solutions for maintaining biodiversity and ecosystem services.
Model why structural changes to genes may affect proteins and an organism's traits.
Model why asexual reproduction yields identical genes while sexual reproduction yields variation.
Model the Earth-sun-moon system to explain lunar phases, eclipses and seasons.
Use rock strata evidence to organize Earth's 4.6-billion-year history.
Explain how geoscience processes change Earth's surface at varying scales.
Model the cycling of water through Earth's systems driven by sunlight and gravity.
Design a method for monitoring and minimizing human impact on the environment.
Ask questions to clarify evidence of factors causing the rise in global temperatures.
Explain how carbon, hydrogen and oxygen from sugars combine with other elements to build amino acids and other large molecules.
Model how interacting systems in multicellular organisms provide specific functions.
Plan and carry out an investigation showing that feedback mechanisms maintain homeostasis in living things.
Model how mitosis and differentiation produce and maintain complex organisms.
Model how photosynthesis transforms light energy into stored chemical energy.
Model how cellular respiration breaks bonds in food and releases energy.
Ask questions about how DNA and chromosomes pass traits from parents to offspring.
Defend a claim that heritable variation comes from meiotic recombination, replication errors and environmentally caused mutations.
Use mathematical representations to explain factors affecting carrying capacity.
Use math to support explanations about biodiversity and populations in ecosystems.
Use math to model the cycling of matter and flow of energy among organisms in an ecosystem.
Evaluate claims that ecosystems stay stable under modest change but can shift under larger ones.
Design, evaluate and refine a solution reducing human impact on the environment and biodiversity.
Evaluate evidence for how group behavior improves individuals' chances of survival and reproduction.
Use the periodic table to predict relative element properties from outermost electron patterns.
Construct explanations of simple chemical reactions using periodic table patterns.
Model how bond energy changes explain whether a reaction releases or absorbs energy.
Explain how changes in temperature or concentration affect reaction rate.
Use math to show that atoms and mass are conserved in a chemical reaction.
Model the changes in nucleus composition and energy released in fission, fusion and decay.
Analyze data to support Newton's second law relating net force, mass and acceleration.
Use math to show that total momentum of a system is conserved when no net external force acts.
Use math to describe and predict gravitational and electrostatic forces between objects.
Use computational models to calculate energy change in a system's components.
Model energy at the macroscopic scale as combined motion and relative-position energy of particles.
Use math to relate wave frequency, wavelength and speed in various media.
Model the sun's life span and how fusion in its core releases energy that reaches Earth as radiation.
Use astronomical evidence, such as redshift and background radiation, to support the Big Bang theory.
Model how Earth's internal and surface processes operate at different scales to form landforms.
Use a model to describe how energy flow variations cause changes in climate.
Model how carbon cycles among the hydrosphere, atmosphere, geosphere and biosphere.
Evaluate or refine a technological solution that reduces human impact on natural systems.
Use the periodic table to predict relative element properties from outermost electron patterns.
Explain simple chemical reactions from periodic table patterns and outer electron states.
Investigate substances' bulk-scale structure and properties to infer the strength of electrical forces between particles.
Explain how temperature and concentration changes affect the rate of a reaction.
Refine a design of a chemical system to increase products at equilibrium.
Use math to show that atoms and mass are conserved in chemical reactions.
Model how bond energy changes explain whether a reaction releases or absorbs energy.
Investigate substances' bulk-scale properties to infer the strength of electrical forces between their particles.
Investigate how combining components at different temperatures in a closed system yields a more uniform energy distribution.
Analyze data to support Newton's second law relating net force, mass and acceleration.
Use math to show momentum is conserved in a system with no net external force.
Design and refine a device that minimizes force on an object during a collision.
Use math to describe and predict gravitational and electrostatic forces between objects.
Use mathematical or computational representations to predict the motion of orbiting objects in the solar system.
Use computational models to calculate energy changes among components of a system.
Model energy at the macroscopic scale as combined particle motion and position energies.
Investigate how thermal energy flows between components at different temperatures toward a more uniform distribution (second law).
Investigate to show electric currents produce magnetic fields and changing magnetic fields produce currents.
Use math to relate wave frequency, wavelength and speed in various media.
Evaluate reasoning that electromagnetic radiation can be modeled as a wave or as particles, each more useful in some situations.
Explain how resource availability, natural hazards and climate change affect human activity.
Evaluate competing designs for developing and managing resources by cost-benefit ratios.
Use a computational simulation to show relationships among resources, population and biodiversity.
Evaluate or refine a technological solution that reduces human impact on natural systems.
Analyze geoscience data and climate model outputs to forecast current or future climate change.
Use a computational model to show how human activity and Earth's systems interact.
Analyze a major global challenge to specify criteria and constraints for solutions.
Design a solution to a complex real-world problem by breaking it into smaller, more manageable problems solvable by engineering.
Evaluate a solution against prioritized criteria and trade-offs, including social and environmental impacts.
Use a computer simulation to model the impact of proposed solutions to a complex problem.
Use models to describe how a wave's amplitude relates to its energy.
Model how waves are reflected, absorbed or transmitted by various materials.
Evaluate evidence that digital signals are more reliable than analog for transmitting information.
Gather information on how sensory receptors send messages to the brain for memory or response.
